summary: Shelf is a very small prototype: one search box, a camera icon, a one-row table, a checkbox and two buttons. Its three actions are not wired, the scan icon and 'Purge all' are not keyboard operable, and the data model has none of the fields the six collector twins rely on (edition, region, location, rip status, condition, price). The visual hierarchy is inverted: the destructive action is loudest and the primary action looks disabled.

findings.title: Every action handler is undefined: scan, Commit and Purge all do nothing
findings.where: Camera icon, Commit button, Purge all
findings.what_happens: scan(), commit() and del() are referenced by onclick but are not defined anywhere in the file (typeof returns 'undefined' for all three in headless Chrome). Clicking each throws a ReferenceError and nothing visible happens. No other script exists.
findings.why_it_matters: No twin can finish any task: scanning, saving a batch, or clearing is impossible. Marcus's and Dale's core jobs (scan 50 discs, check a title in a store) start at the scan control.
findings.recommendation: If this is a deliberate prototype stub, wire each control to a visible placeholder result (a toast, a fake result row) so walkthroughs and real-user tests exercise the flow. Otherwise implement the three handlers.

findings.title: Scan control is a 20x17 emoji span: no keyboard access, no name, tiny target
findings.what_happens: The scan trigger is a <span class='icon' onclick> containing a camera emoji. It has no tabindex, no role, no accessible name, and is not in the tab order (only the search input, checkbox and Commit are focusable). Rendered size is 20x17 px with no gap from the search box. The 16x16 CSS size is overridden by the inline emoji.
findings.why_it_matters: Keyboard and screen reader users cannot scan at all. Marcus, Dale and Kenji rely on scanning, often one-handed in a store; Dale's evidence reports black-screen scanners and awkward small-screen apps, so a 17 px target adds to that. Walt may not recognise an unlabelled icon and avoids camera-dependent flows.
findings.recommendation: Option A: a real <button type='button'> with a visible 'Scan' label and an aria-label, min 44x44 on touch. Option B: icon plus text button placed first in the row, with typed UPC entry beside it. Keep it consistent with the app's button styling.

findings.title: 'Purge all' is an unguarded destructive action styled as plain red text
findings.what_happens: 'Purge all' is a <div onclick>, not a button. It sits directly under Commit with no gap, has no confirmation, undo or scope (purge what: the queue, the collection?), is not keyboard reachable, and has no pointer cursor. Red (#ff0000) on white is 4.0:1.
findings.why_it_matters: For Walt, Marcus (hundreds to thousands of discs) and Rosa (thousands ripped over years) an accidental purge means losing years of cataloguing; Marcus also distrusts anything he cannot export. A mis-tap beside the primary button is likely on a phone.
findings.recommendation: Option A: rename to a specific verb such as 'Clear queue', make it a secondary text button, separate it from Commit, and confirm with a count ('Remove 1 item?'). Option B: no confirm but a 10-second Undo toast. Do not offer 'purge all' at collection level without export first. Use a red of at least 4.5:1 (for example #b3261e is about 6.5:1).

findings.title: Emphasis is inverted: the destructive action is loudest, the primary action looks disabled
findings.what_happens: Commit is a grey (#ddd) 13px button with no border, 1.36:1 against the white page. Purge all is saturated red 16px text. The h1 'Shelf' is 14px, smaller than the 16px body and table text, so the page title is the quietest thing on screen. The eye lands on the red text first.
findings.why_it_matters: Users decide what is safe from visual weight. Walt is easily lost on dense screens; Marcus scans quickly and will hit what stands out.
findings.recommendation: Make Commit (or the renamed primary) the one filled, high-contrast button; render Purge/Clear as a quiet secondary; set the h1 above body size (about 24px). Offer two or three directions for the page structure to the design team: single-column queue list, or table plus sticky action bar.

findings.title: The only instruction line is #bbb at 11px (1.92:1 contrast)
findings.where: Hint text 'Ingest queue: reconcile metadata before commit'
findings.what_happens: Colour #bbbbbb on #ffffff computes to 1.92:1 at 11px. It is the only explanatory text on the page. Body text (#222 on white) is 15.9:1, so this is an isolated failure.
findings.why_it_matters: Walt's documented pain is text he cannot read or enlarge; he will miss the only guidance. Everyone else will also skip it, so the screen loses its only orientation.
findings.recommendation: Raise to at least #595959 (about 7:1) and at least 14px, or fold the guidance into a heading and plain sentence. Do not rely on grey for text that tells people what to do.

findings.title: Internal jargon: 'Ingest queue', 'reconcile metadata', 'Commit', 'Fmt', 'SKU', 'BD'
findings.what_happens: Copy reads like a developer's data pipeline. 'Fmt' is an abbreviation of a word that fits on screen; 'SKU' shows 0883929 where collectors say UPC or barcode; 'Commit' does not say what is being saved; 'BD' is not defined; 'Purge all' is unclear in scope.
findings.why_it_matters: Walt avoids 'sync', 'database', 'cloud'-style terms. Marcus's vocabulary is 'UPC', 'scan', 'import'. Dale and Kenji use 'pressing' and 'variant', Priya 'edition'/'label'. Nobody's vocabulary list contains 'ingest' or 'reconcile' (Rosa tolerates technical terms but wants 'rip' and 'library').
findings.recommendation: Use collector words: 'Review new discs', 'Format', 'Barcode (UPC)', 'Save to collection', 'Blu-ray'. Let Rosa-style technical terms live in an optional detail view rather than the default screen.

findings.title: No way to add, import or batch-enter titles
findings.what_happens: The page has a search box, a scan trigger and one hard-coded row (Alien, BD, 0883929). There is no add form, no manual entry, no import (CSV, file, paste), and nothing that explains how rows get into the 'queue'.
findings.why_it_matters: Entry effort is the top abandonment reason in the twins' evidence: Marcus (10,000+ titles by hand felt impossible), Walt (family helper entering titles), Kenji (import titles missing from databases), Rosa (add unripped discs as placeholders).
findings.recommendation: Offer at least: manual add with a typed barcode field, paste-a-list/CSV import, and a free-text entry for titles not found. Put them in the first screen of the queue.

findings.title: Record has no release-level fields: edition, label, spine/catalog no., pressing, region, variant
findings.what_happens: A row is Title + Fmt + SKU. 'Alien / BD' cannot say which release (original, Criterion, 4K, steelbook), which pressing, or which region.
findings.why_it_matters: Priya's whole job is the exact release and spine number; Dale thinks in pressings and says 'album' is the wrong unit; Kenji must record NTSC-J/PAL and variants; Rosa wants label and catalog fields she can sort. Evidence in several communities shows people leave tools that cannot hold these fields.
findings.recommendation: Add a Release block (label, catalog/spine number, release year, country/region, edition notes) plus Region and Variant. Use one visible term ('Release') and offer synonyms in help text because the twins disagree on 'edition' vs 'pressing' vs 'variant' (see tensions).

findings.title: Nothing links a disc to where it is or whether it is ripped or lent
findings.what_happens: The only state on a disc is the 'Mark as sealed' checkbox. There is no shelf or box location, no ripped/not ripped status, no link to a media-server library entry, and no loan record.
findings.why_it_matters: Rosa's single source of truth is 'on the shelf, on the NAS, or both?' and 'where is this box?'. Without it she keeps a separate catalog beside her media server.
findings.recommendation: Add Location (free text and suggestions), Ripped status (not ripped, ripped, better disc available) and optional On loan to. Keep them optional and hidden behind an expander so casual collectors are not slowed.

findings.title: No purchase price, store, date or condition grade
findings.what_happens: No fields exist to record price paid, store, purchase date or condition (record and sleeve grade, disc condition).
findings.why_it_matters: Marcus wants price/store/date; Dale grades record and sleeve as he adds; Walt needs condition and approximate value for downsizing, insurance and heirs, and the evidence says grade-as-you-add saves time later.
findings.recommendation: Add optional Price, Store, Date and Condition fields with a short grade picker (Mint to Poor). Make value display opt-in because some collectors do not want it (see tensions).

findings.title: No sorting, filtering or owned/missing views
findings.what_happens: The table has plain headers, no sort control, no filter by format/label/region, and the search box has no stated scope (title? SKU?).
findings.why_it_matters: Priya, Rosa and Kenji each describe abandoning tools whose label or region fields could not be sorted or filtered; all three need views like 'everything from this label in spine order' or 'every Japanese release for one platform'.
findings.recommendation: Make headers sortable buttons with aria-sort, add filter chips for Format and Region, and state the search scope in its label ('Search title or barcode').

findings.title: No export, print or inventory view
findings.what_happens: There is no CSV/XML export, no print layout and no sharable list.
findings.why_it_matters: Marcus distrusts anything he cannot export and wants to be able to leave; Walt needs a printable inventory for insurance and heirs; Rosa wants import/export, not another silo.
findings.recommendation: Add Export (CSV) and a plain print stylesheet for a simple list. Place it in the main toolbar, not in settings.

findings.title: In-store 'do I already own this?' path is unclear
findings.what_happens: Search shows no results area, no 'owned' indicator, no duplicate warning, and nothing about offline use or what happens when a barcode is not found. Only the one hard-coded row exists.
findings.why_it_matters: Checking duplicates in a shop is the main use case for Marcus, Dale (with unreliable signal at fairs) and Kenji (PAL vs NTSC copies). Marcus's evidence says about 6% of UPCs are not found.
findings.recommendation: Show a clear result state ('You own this: Alien, Blu-ray, shelf B3' / 'Not in your collection'), a not-found path that offers manual add, and an offline notice. Test with real scanning in a shop.

findings.title: Search is placeholder-only; the field has no visible label and unclear scope
findings.what_happens: <input placeholder='Search'> has no <label>, aria-label or id. The placeholder disappears on typing. Placeholder colour computes to about 4.6:1 and the field is 21px high with 13.3px text.
findings.why_it_matters: Walt and anyone in a hurry in a store lose the cue once they type; the scope (title, barcode, label) is never stated.
findings.recommendation: Add a visible label or an aria-label plus a persistent hint, ensure at least 16px text and a 44px touch height, and set type='search'.

findings.title: 'Mark as sealed' is an unstyled 13px checkbox with unclear scope
findings.what_happens: A default-styled browser checkbox (13x13) with a label (133x17). It is not tied to a row, so it is unclear whether it marks the Alien row, a selection or the whole queue. Neighbours (Commit, Purge) sit directly below, so the 24px spacing exception probably fails.
findings.why_it_matters: Default controls clash with the app's own flat styling; Walt needs bigger hit areas. Kenji tracks loose/boxed/complete/sealed, a single boolean cannot hold that.
findings.recommendation: Option A: restyle the checkbox to the app's look at 24px with a 44px row hit area, placed in each row. Option B: replace with a 'Condition/Completeness' select (Sealed, Complete, Boxed, Loose). Never ship it in default browser styling.

findings.title: Commit button is 23px tall, 1.36:1 against the page, with no feedback or states
findings.what_happens: Button is 54x23 CSS px with 4px padding, grey #ddd fill on white (1.36:1), no border, and no defined hover, disabled or loading style. Because the handler is undefined, no success or failure message exists.
findings.why_it_matters: The primary action looks disabled; Walt and one-handed phone users miss or mistime the tap, and nobody learns whether the commit worked (Rosa and Marcus commit batches of 30-50).
findings.recommendation: Give it at least 44px height, a filled accent colour with 4.5:1 text, a visible focus style, a pressed state, and a status message announced via role='status' ('12 discs saved').

findings.title: Document structure: no lang, no landmarks, a 14px h1, no section headings
findings.what_happens: <html> has no lang attribute; there is no <main>, header or nav; h1 is 14px (smaller than body); the table has no caption and no scope on <th>; the search, queue and actions are not grouped under headings.
findings.why_it_matters: Screen-reader users get no page language or regions; Walt (low vision, possibly using a reader or zoom) is easily lost without structure.
findings.recommendation: Add lang='en', wrap content in <main>, make h1 about 24px, add h2s ('Search', 'Queue', 'Actions'), a table caption and scope='col' on headers.

findings.title: No viewport meta tag: the page will render at desktop width on phones
findings.what_happens: The head has only a title and style; there is no <meta name='viewport'>. Mobile browsers will lay the page out at about 980px and shrink it, making 11-16px text and 13-20px controls tiny. Not verified on a real phone (see not run).
findings.why_it_matters: Marcus, Dale and Kenji do the check in a shop on a phone; Dale's evidence describes small-screen apps as awkward.
findings.recommendation: Add <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width,initial-scale=1'>, and test at 320 px and 200% zoom after layout work.

findings.title: Inconsistent type scale and an unstructured table
findings.what_happens: Font sizes in use: 11px (hint), 13.3px (input and button), 14px (h1), 16px (table, label). The table has no borders, row separators, zebra or column widths, so the three columns sit tightly together (see Title/Fmt/SKU). A single row hides how it will look at hundreds of rows.
findings.why_it_matters: Priya, Rosa and Marcus scan long lists and need legible columns; Walt needs a consistent, larger base size.
findings.recommendation: Adopt a type scale (for example 16/18/24) with a minimum of 16px for inputs, add row dividers and a sticky header, and test the table with 200+ rows.

tensions: Rich release-level fields (Priya, Dale, Kenji, Rosa) versus Walt's need for a plain, large-text list that does not overwhelm him: use a simple default row with an expandable detail section.
Camera/scan-first entry (Marcus, Dale, Kenji) versus Walt, who may have no camera or scanner and relies on a family member typing: typed barcode and paste-a-list entry need to be equal citizens.

Vocabulary clash: Priya says 'edition' and 'release', Dale says 'pressing' (and may read 'edition' as ambiguous), Kenji says 'variant' and 'platform', Rosa reads 'collection' as a Plex grouping: no single label suits all, so pick one and add synonyms in help text.

Value and price tracking: Marcus wants price paid and Walt wants approximate value, but Kenji's evidence describes value tracking as anxiety-inducing for some: make price and value optional, off by default for display.
A single 'sealed' flag is enough for Marcus and Walt but too coarse for Kenji's loose/boxed/complete/sealed ladder.
Technical wording ('ingest', 'metadata', 'rip') is natural for Rosa but excludes Walt: default plain, allow technical labels on detail views.
what_works: Body text is #222 on white (15.9:1) and uses real text, so it scales with browser zoom without fixed widths.
Native input, checkbox and button keep the browser's default focus ring (the CSS does not remove outlines), and they are in the tab order.
The checkbox is wrapped in a <label>, so clicking its words toggles it, and the data is in a real <table> with <th> header cells.
The 'Alien / BD / barcode' row shows the right idea: title, format and barcode in one scannable line.
A single h1 exists, and the layout is a single column with no horizontal scroll at the 780px width tested.

open_questions.question: Do collectors reach for scanning or typed search first when checking a title in a store?
open_questions.method: Intercept screener plus 5 short in-store sessions with Marcus/Dale/Kenji-like collectors
open_questions.why: Twins disagree on whether scan or search is primary; affects layout of the first screen.

open_questions.question: Which word do people expect for the exact release: edition, release, pressing or variant?
open_questions.method: Card sort and first-click test with 8-10 collectors across discs, vinyl and games

open_questions.question: How much detail will older, low-vision collectors tolerate on the add screen?
open_questions.method: Moderated think-aloud with 5 participants aged 65+ at 200% zoom and a screen magnifier
open_questions.why: Walt is a moderate-evidence hypothesis; his accessibility need is backed by only two sources.

open_questions.question: Do people want price or value shown, hidden or absent?
Does 'Purge all' / 'Commit' cause real errors?
open_questions.method: Unmoderated task test on a clickable prototype with 8 users
open_questions.why: Severity is inferred from forum evidence about data loss, not observed behaviour.

limits: Twins are synthetic hypotheses built from vocal online communities (version 0.1, status hypothesis, no real-user validation) and over-represent complaints. The prototype is tiny and its handlers are undefined, so interaction-level findings are inferred from code and the twins' documented behaviour. Walt's low-vision profile rests on two sources. Contrast ratios and element sizes were computed from source and headless Chrome; screen readers, real mobile devices, and 320px reflow were not tested.
